question: Can a class-balanced gradient-boosting model that ranks type states by predicted bug yield find more seeded bugs within a fixed run budget than a type-coverage queue that treats every new type state equally?
method: Seeded simulation of fuzzing campaigns. Type states have feature vectors; a small fraction hide bugs with low per-run trigger probability. A class-balanced LightGBM trained on earlier campaigns scores type states; the same queue and run budget are used for both schedulers. Campaigns are split once into train and test; tuning uses 3-fold CV on training rows only.
metric_name: distinct seeded bugs found within fixed run budget (mean per test campaign)
baseline: Type-coverage-guided queue: round-robin over type states in first-come order, every new type state has equal priority.
improved: Same queue and budget, but each run goes to the queued type state with the highest class-balanced LightGBM bug-yield score (discounted by runs spent).
notes: Simulation only; the hidden bug signal is linear in the features, which favours the tree model, so gains may be optimistic. Training labels come from baseline-style campaigns. Campaign-level split (not row-stratified) to avoid leakage. Bugs are rare, so the metric is noisy; standard deviations are across three seeds.
